topic: How a foreign buyer purchases property in Greece, step by step
facts: Every buyer needs a Greek tax number (AFM) before signing; non-residents can get it through a tax representative or a lawyer with power of attorney.
A Greek bank account is normally needed, because the price must be paid by traceable bank transfer, not cash.
The buyer's own lawyer checks the title deeds and the Hellenic Cadastre (Ktimatologio) record of the property.
An engineer checks the building permit and whether there are unauthorised constructions that must be legalised before the sale.
An Energy Performance Certificate (PEA) is required for every sale.
A preliminary agreement with a deposit can be signed before the final contract.
The final purchase contract is signed before a notary public; the transfer tax is paid before signing.
After signing, the contract is registered at the Hellenic Cadastre; only then is the buyer the registered owner.
The whole purchase can be done from abroad through a power of attorney given to a lawyer.

topic: Greek tax number (AFM) and bank account for buying property
facts: The AFM is the Greek tax identification number; it is required to buy property, sign a lease or open utility contracts.
Non-EU residents usually need a tax representative in Greece to obtain and use an AFM.
A lawyer can apply for the AFM on the buyer's behalf with a power of attorney.
Greek banks ask non-residents for a passport, the AFM, proof of address abroad and proof of the source of funds.
The purchase price must be paid by bank transfer or banker's cheque so that the payment can be traced; this is stated in the contract.
Opening a bank account as a non-resident can take several weeks, so it is best started early.

topic: The costs of buying property in Greece, explained
facts: For resale properties the property transfer tax is 3% of the taxable value, plus a municipal surcharge of 3% on that tax, so 3.09% in total.
The taxable value is the higher of the price in the contract and the official 'objective value' of the property.
Notary fees are roughly 0.8% to 1% of the value, plus VAT.
The buyer's lawyer usually charges roughly 1% of the price, plus VAT, or an agreed fixed fee.
Registration at the Hellenic Cadastre costs roughly 0.5% of the value plus small fixed fees.
New-build properties can be subject to VAT instead of transfer tax, depending on the building permit date; this must be checked for each property.
Owners pay an annual property tax called ENFIA, which depends on the size, location and age of the property.
An estate agent's fee is agreed in writing before viewings.

topic: Greece Golden Visa: the property investment thresholds by area
facts: The Greek Golden Visa gives a five-year renewable residence permit to non-EU citizens who buy property in Greece.
Since 2024 the minimum investment is EUR 800,000 in Attica (including Athens), Thessaloniki, Mykonos, Santorini and islands with more than 3,100 residents.
In the rest of Greece the minimum is EUR 400,000.
A EUR 250,000 option exists only for converting a commercial building into residences or restoring a listed building.
For the EUR 800,000 and EUR 400,000 options the investment must be in a single property of at least 120 m².
Properties bought for the Golden Visa cannot be rented out as short-term rentals such as Airbnb; long-term leases are allowed.
The permit covers the investor's spouse and children, and the holder does not have to live in Greece to keep it.
Rules change from time to time, so the current rules are confirmed with a lawyer before each purchase.

topic: What we check before you buy a property in Greece
facts: The title deeds show who owns the property and how they acquired it; the buyer's lawyer traces them back over the years.
The Hellenic Cadastre (Ktimatologio) record must match the deeds, the size and the boundaries of the property.
The lawyer checks for mortgages, seizures, liens or court cases on the property.
An engineer compares the property with its building permit and plans; unauthorised additions must be legalised before the sale.
The seller provides an Energy Performance Certificate (PEA), which is required for every sale and lease.
Building common charges and any unpaid utility bills are checked so the buyer does not inherit debts.
In apartment buildings, the building regulations are read to see what uses are allowed, for example short-term rentals or offices.

topic: Buying property in Greece from abroad with a power of attorney
facts: A buyer does not need to travel to Greece to sign; a lawyer in Greece can sign the contract with a power of attorney.
The power of attorney can be signed at a Greek consulate abroad or before a local notary with an Apostille stamp, followed by an official translation.
The power of attorney must state exactly what the lawyer may do, for example get the AFM, open a bank account and sign the purchase contract.
Viewings can be done by live video call, so the buyer sees the property in real time.
The buyer approves each step, and the payment is made by bank transfer to the seller's account, as written in the contract.

topic: Long-term rental or Airbnb in Athens: how to choose
facts: A long-term lease gives a steady monthly income and little day-to-day work for the owner.
Short-term rentals such as Airbnb can earn more in good months but have more costs: cleaning, laundry, guest communication, platform commissions and furnishing.
Every short-term rental in Greece must be registered and display its registry number (AMA) in the listing.
Some central Athens areas have had restrictions on new short-term rental registrations, so the current rules are checked for each address.
Properties bought for the Golden Visa cannot be used as short-term rentals.
Building regulations can forbid short-term rentals in a specific apartment building.

topic: Tax on rental income in Greece for property owners
facts: Rental income from property in Greece is taxed in Greece, also when the owner lives abroad.
Rental income is taxed at 15% up to EUR 12,000 a year, 35% from EUR 12,001 to EUR 35,000 and 45% above EUR 35,000, according to the rates in force.
Every lease must be declared on the Greek tax platform (Taxisnet) by the landlord.
Owners file a Greek income tax return every year when they have rental income in Greece.
Double tax treaties can prevent the same income being taxed twice; an accountant confirms how this applies in each country.

topic: The Athens Riviera for families: Glyfada and Voula
facts: Glyfada and Voula are coastal suburbs south of central Athens, on the Athens Riviera.
Glyfada has a large shopping and restaurant centre, a marina and golf course.
Voula is quieter and more residential, with organised beaches and villas with gardens.
The coastal tram connects Glyfada and Voula with the centre of Athens.
Both areas have international and private schools nearby.
S.F. Properties is selling a new garden maisonette with a private pool in Voula.

topic: Central Athens for investors: Koukaki, Pagkrati and Petralona
facts: Koukaki and Makrygianni are next to the Acropolis Museum and very popular with visitors.
Pagkrati is a lively residential neighbourhood near the Panathenaic Stadium, popular with young professionals.
Petralona sits next to Filopappou Hill and has a metro station on line 1.
Older apartments in central Athens are often renovated before being rented out.
Demand for long-term rentals in central Athens comes from students, professionals and people moving to Athens.
Before buying for short-term rental, the current registration rules for the specific address are checked.

topic: Renting a home in Athens as a foreigner: what you need
facts: Tenants need a Greek tax number (AFM) to sign a lease, because the landlord declares the lease on Taxisnet.
A passport or EU identity card is required.
Landlords usually ask for a deposit, often equal to one or two months' rent, plus the first month's rent.
Residential leases in Greece commonly last at least three years by law, even if a shorter term is written, unless an exception applies.
The tenant usually pays electricity, water and the share of building common charges for daily use.
Viewings can be arranged in person or by video call for people still abroad.

topic: Managing your property in Greece from abroad
facts: A property manager finds and checks tenants, signs the lease and registers it on Taxisnet with the accountant.
The manager collects the rent and pays bills, common charges and property taxes for the owner.
Repairs and maintenance are arranged with trusted technicians, and the owner approves costs.
Owners receive regular statements of income and expenses.
For short-term rentals the manager also handles listings, pricing, cleaning and guests.
